title: Will AI Replace Finance Jobs? What’s Changing, What’s at Risk, and What’s Next
summary: Will AI replace finance jobs? Learn which roles are the most vulnerable, skills that remain irreplaceable, and what the next decade looks like.

- Will AI Replace Finance Jobs? What’s Changing, What’s at Risk, and What’s Next


The reality of the modern financial sector is that AI is already deeply embedded in daily workflows. It summarizes dense documents. It extracts data from corporate proxy statements. It flags transaction anomalies for fraud detection. The list goes on.


So, the real question isn’t whether AI will change the financial industry. That ship has long since sailed. The more pressing concern for today’s professionals is this: Will AI replace finance jobs entirely? Or, more accurately, which specific roles will it reshape and replace? And which human skills will become exponentially more valuable because of it?


Drawing on research and reporting from the World Economic Forum (WEF), US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Goldman Sachs, Bloomberg, Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) Institute, InvestmentNews, TD Bank, Intuit Credit Karma, CNBC, Gallup, Experian, and Accenture, this piece breaks down the data to show what the coming years hold for financial careers.


## **Key Takeaways**


- **Global AI exposure:** Generative AI could expose the equivalent of 300 million full-time jobs globally to automation.


- **The back-office decline:** Operational and administrative roles face the highest automation risk, with the BLS projecting a loss of nearly 762,000 office and administrative support jobs nationwide between 2024 and 2034.


- **Steady demand for human advisors:** Despite the proliferation of automated “robo-advisors,” personal financial advisor roles are projected to grow by a massive 17.1%.


- **The trust deficit:** While 78% of Americans currently use AI tools in their daily lives, only 18% trust AI to make financial recommendations on its own.


- **Evolution over elimination:** Demand for financial analysts and accountants is projected to grow by 6% and 5%, respectively, through 2034.


- **The new baseline skill:** AI proficiency is becoming a must-have career skill, with over 90% of recent finance graduates recognizing that mastering these tools will benefit their career prospects.


## **How Is AI Reshaping Finance Jobs?**


Finance has absorbed major technology shifts before. Ledgers gave way to calculators, then Excel, then Python. Each transition reshaped daily work without breaking the industry.


AI is different. It moves faster and handles cognitive work that earlier tools couldn’t, including synthesizing data and drafting analysis. The broader story of[how AI impacts finance](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/tech-innovation/artificial-intelligence-in-finance/) goes well beyond job displacement, but the labor market effects tell a story.


The scale is what makes this shift hard to ignore:

The risk of AI taking over finance jobs lands hardest on entry-level work. Junior analysts have traditionally earned their spot by doing the grunt work, like pulling data from filings and summarizing research.[AI in fintech](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/tech-innovation/fintech-artificial-intelligence/) handles those tasks in seconds.


That changes the career ladder. The industry is shifting away from rewarding basic data production and toward valuing what AI still can’t do well, such as interpreting nuance and shaping strategy.


## **Which Finance Roles Are Most at Risk?**


AI exposure in finance isn’t uniform. Some roles are projected to grow despite AI adoption. Others are already shrinking. The difference comes down to how much of the work involves routine cognitive tasks AI can replicate versus judgment and accountability that still require a person.

### **Will AI Replace Financial Advisors?**


For those questioning whether AI will replace finance jobs, the picture of personal financial advising employment suggests that’s unlikely.


While app-based robo-advisors can successfully automate a good chunk of core portfolio management and wealth allocation tasks, the demand for human advisors is projected to hold steady. According to the BLS, there were 321,000 personal financial advisor roles available in 2023, and that number is expected to jump by 17.1% to nearly 376,000 by 2033.


Advising’s projected stability likely comes down to trust. A recent[TD Bank survey](https://stories.td.com/us/en/article/nearly-80-of-americans-use-ai-tools-but-most-still-want-humans-making-financial-decisions-td-survey-finds) found that while nearly 80% of Americans use AI tools in their daily lives, 18% trust AI to make financial recommendations on its own. Consumers seem comfortable with letting AI handle tasks like tracking spending and detecting fraud. But they still take comfort in human accountability when the stakes are high.


The future of financial advising is likely to look something like this: AI handles the speed and back-end math. Humans manage the relationship-building and ethical duties of care that come with managing someone else’s life savings.


### **Will AI Replace Financial Analysts?**


Financial analysts provide a case for evolution rather than elimination. There were 429,000 financial analyst roles available in the US, according to the BLS. The agency predicts that number will grow by 6% by 2034, adding more than 25,000 jobs along the way.


AI is already managing a lot of the manual grunt work previously assigned to junior analysts. That includes tasks like extracting governance details from proxy statements or synthesizing massive datasets.


What hasn’t changed is that someone has to verify the output and catch what the model misses. As the[CFA Institute](https://rpc.cfainstitute.org/blogs/enterprising-investor/2025/ai-can-pass-the-cfa-exam-but-it-cannot-replace-analysts) notes, an AI can pass a structured finance exam, but it can’t apply nuanced judgment to unpredictable, real-world market events.


That means the future will likely involve some form of an AI + HI (human intelligence) model. Instead of spending hours crunching numbers, analyst work will probably center more on strategic data interpretation and identifying the market outliers that machines miss.


In other words, the grunt work moves to machines. The interpretation stays with people.


### **Will AI Replace Accountants and Bookkeepers?**


AI is likely to replace basic bookkeeping and data-entry roles, but strategic accountants have staying power.


Jobs reliant entirely on routine manual processing are at high risk, which is why office and administrative support occupations broadly[are projected to decline](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/ecopro.pdf) by 3.9%, shedding more than 760,000 jobs by 2034. Conversely, there were roughly 1.59 million accountant and auditor roles in 2025, and that number is[projected to grow](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/business-and-financial/accountants-and-auditors.htm) by 5% by 2034.


The reason higher-level work holds up is accountability. AI platforms can generate financial statements, but they can’t sign off on them. And they can’t be held legally responsible for corporate disclosures or take the call when something goes sideways with a regulator. That’s why human oversight remains mandatory in scenarios like these.


It helps to think about[AI’s impact on accounting](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/how-will-ai-affect-accounting) as akin to that of a powerful assistant. Automating routine reconciliation and data entry makes accountants exponentially more efficient. And that’s likely to pave the way toward a future of high-level advisory and strategic consulting duties.


## **New Finance Jobs AI Is Creating**


While much of the conversation focuses on automation, artificial intelligence is creating new career paths. As major banks and investment firms incorporate machine learning into much of what they do, a[CFA Institute report](https://www.cfainstitute.org/insights/articles/ai-finance-graduates-optimistic-career-prospects) revealed that the single most in-demand talent across the industry today is finance professionals with AI and big data skills.


As financial institutions invest in AI and redesign core workflows, several roles are becoming more important across analysis, compliance, risk, and data infrastructure. The exact titles vary by company, but the skill sets are easy to spot:


- **AI strategist/AI-integrated analyst:** Moving away from manual data extraction, these analysts master the AI + HI model. They focus on interrogating AI outputs and applying nuanced judgment to drive strategic investment decisions.
- **Model risk and AI governance specialist** : With the rapid deployment of generative models, firms require specialists to evaluate technological threats and limit potential losses. These experts establish guardrails against unique machine learning risks, such as AI hallucinations and intellectual property infringement.
- **AI ethicist/fair-lending compliance officer:** Financial firms using AI in lending, credit scoring, investment advice, or customer interactions need professionals who can read both the technology and the regulations governing it. The work means making sure AI systems hold up against frameworks like the[Equal Credit Opportunity Act](https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/statutes/equal-credit-opportunity-act) and the comprehensive[EU AI Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/) , and catching algorithmic bias before it produces real-world harm.
- **Financial data engineer/database architect:** Training and deploying sophisticated AI engines requires massive amounts of organized data and cloud computing power. Firms are actively hiring architects to build and maintain this complex data infrastructure, a role the BLS projects will grow by 10.8% over the next decade.
- **Agentic AI workflow designer:** Anticipating how agentic AI will transform financial services, these designers build advanced systems that incorporate chain-of-thought reasoning and external function calling. They create AI application layers that interface with traditional software, expanding what machines can automate while maintaining human oversight. The work also extends into[AI training](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/how-to-train-ai-model/) itself, fine-tuning models on financial workflows so they perform reliably in production.


## **How Intuit Sees the Shift in AI and Financial Careers**


Intuit’s approach reflects what the data shows. The most useful applications of AI in financial services keep humans in the loop where it matters.


Intuit Intelligence powers personalized financial guidance across TurboTax, Credit Karma, QuickBooks, and Mailchimp, combining AI automation with embedded access to trusted human experts. Those capabilities now reach customers inside the AI platforms they already use:


- [Anthropic](https://www.intuit.com/blog/news-social/intuit-apps-now-available-in-claude/) **:** Intuit apps are available in Claude, bringing QuickBooks workflows into the assistant businesses are already working in.
- [OpenAI](https://www.intuit.com/chatgpt/) : Intuit’s ChatGPT integration connects conversations to tax and business tools without leaving the chat.
- [Perplexity](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/tech-innovation/intuit-perplexity-partnership/) **:** QuickBooks and Mailchimp run inside Perplexity Computer, so businesses can chase overdue invoices, retrieve payroll information, and track campaign performance from a single workflow.
- [Meta](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/tech-innovation/intuit-quickbooks-joins-muse-for-small-business/) **:** QuickBooks is a launch partner in Muse, from Meta, where owners can review cash flow, benchmark their balance sheet against industry peers, and send payment-enabled invoices.


AI handles the speed and the personalization. People handle the high-stakes calls and the compliance review. That shape of work is what the next generation of financial careers looks like: AI raising the floor on what financial professionals need to know and rewarding the people who treat AI fluency as a foundational skill they keep building on.

A WEF/Accenture report says AI investment across those sub-sectors is[projected to rise from $35 billion in 2023 to $97 billion by 2027](https://reports.weforum.org/docs/WEF_Artificial_Intelligence_in_Financial_Services_2025.pdf) , with banking, insurance, and capital markets showing high automation and augmentation potential.
